sections.value: Choosing a coding agent is two decisions, and almost nobody notices the second one. The first is the **model** — Opus, GPT-5.6, Kimi. The second is the **harness**: the program wrapped around the model that hands it tools, decides what goes into its context window, and runs the loop until the work is done. Claude Code is a harness. Codex CLI is a harness. The model supplies the intelligence; the harness decides how it gets used.

A team from UC Berkeley and Arena went and measured what that second decision is
worth. In [HarnessTax](https://harnesstax.github.io/) they take seven models and run each one
through three harnesses — Claude Code, Codex CLI, and a minimal open-source harness called
Pi — on the same tasks drawn from SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2.0. Twenty-one
model–harness pairs, thirty tasks apiece, three attempts per task.

The result is awkward for anyone who has been treating the harness as a detail:

> Claude Fable 5 resolves **96.7%** of SWE-bench Lite attempts running in Pi, and **97.8%**
> running in Claude Code — a gap of about one task in ninety. The Pi run costs **$0.67** per
> attempt. The Claude Code run costs **$1.33**.

Same model. Same tasks. Same answers, near enough. Twice the bill. The authors call the
difference a **harness tax**, and their argument is that most people are paying one without
ever having been shown the invoice.

## What is actually being compared

A harness is the software loop around a model. It decides which tools the model may call, what
the system prompt says, how files and command output are folded back into the conversation,
when to compact or summarise, and when to stop. Three of them here:

| Harness | Shape |
|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Anthropic's agent. 23 tools declared on the first call, including subagents, planning and task management. |
| **Codex CLI** | OpenAI's agent. Around 7 tools. |
| **Pi** | A minimal open-source harness. Four tools: `read`, `write`, `edit`, `bash`. |

And two benchmarks. **SWE-bench Lite** is real GitHub issues from Python repositories, where the
agent has to produce a patch that makes the project's own tests pass. **Terminal-Bench 2.0** is
harder and less tidy: realistic command-line tasks judged by their end state.

The measurement detail that makes the comparison mean anything is the pricing. Costs are
**standardised** — token counts run through one fixed direct-API price list, with the same
prices applied to a model in every harness. So a cost difference in these charts is never a
discount or a subscription artefact. It is the harness having spent more tokens to get to the
same place.

## Finding 1: the harness moves the bill, not the score

Read the two panels against each other. Up top, holding the model fixed and swapping
the harness moves the success rate by a couple of points — often less than the noise on a
30-task sample. Down below, the same swap moves cost by **2×**, **3.5×**, once by **5×**.

Across the models they share, the study puts Claude Code at about **2.0×** the cost of Pi and
**1.6×** the cost of Codex CLI on SWE-bench Lite, and **1.5×** Pi on Terminal-Bench 2.0
(geometric means of the per-model ratios). Meanwhile the average effect of the harness on
success rate stays inside **±2 points** on SWE-bench Lite and about **±5 points** on
Terminal-Bench 2.0.

That asymmetry is the whole finding. Correctness is roughly a property of the model. Cost is
very much a property of the harness.

## Finding 2: four tools gets you most of the way

The Pareto frontier is the set of systems that nothing else beats on both axes at once — no
other pair is simultaneously cheaper *and* better. Everything not on it is strictly dominated:
there is a system you could switch to that is better and costs less. Here is the frontier on
SWE-bench Lite, all seven of them:

| System | Resolved | Cost per attempt |
|---|---|---|
| GPT-5.6 Luna · **Pi** | 53.3% | $0.030 |
| GPT-5.6 Luna · Codex CLI | 55.6% | $0.035 |
| Claude Haiku 4.5 · **Pi** | 60.0% | $0.374 |
| GPT-5.6 Sol · **Pi** | 74.4% | $0.441 |
| Claude Opus 4.8 · **Pi** | 82.2% | $0.473 |
| Claude Fable 5 · **Pi** | 96.7% | $0.666 |
| Claude Fable 5 · Claude Code | 97.8% | $1.329 |

The four-tool harness holds **five of the seven seats**. On Terminal-Bench 2.0 the frontier is
only two systems wide, and Pi holds **both**. The single most expensive system on SWE-bench
Lite, GPT-5.6 Sol in Claude Code at **$1.540** per attempt, is beaten on success rate by six
other pairs — three of which cost less than half as much.

So where does the money go? Some of it is gone before the model has read a word of the task.

Claude Code opens the conversation with **13.7×** as much context as Pi. That prefix
is not paid once; it is carried through every turn of the run.

And the extra context is not buying extra work. For Claude Fable 5 on SWE-bench Lite, Pi and
Claude Code take almost exactly the same number of turns per attempt — **15.4** and **15.3**.
Same model, same task, same number of steps, twice the money. The difference is what each step
costs to take.

There is a genuinely encouraging reading of this for anyone building agents. You do not need
privileged access to a frontier lab's harness, or a model co-trained with your scaffolding, to
be competitive on these benchmarks. `read`, `write`, `edit`, `bash` and a decent model gets you
onto the frontier.

## Finding 3: your model may prefer someone else's harness

Providers do tune models for their own environments — OpenAI has described GPT-5-Codex as
optimised for agentic software engineering inside Codex. The reasonable expectation is that a
model does its best work at home.

It mostly does not. Claude Sonnet 4.6 resolves **68.9%** in Codex CLI against
**66.7%** in Claude Code on SWE-bench Lite, at much the same cost. GPT-5.6 Sol on
Terminal-Bench 2.0 reaches **83.3%** in Pi against **78.9%** in Codex CLI — and does it for
roughly half the money, **$0.42** against **$0.76**.

The useful way to read this is not that anyone's harness is bad. It is that a model's
capability travels. It is not locked to the environment it shipped with, so the pairing is a
real decision with a real spread, and the default is not reliably the right end of it.

## What to take from it

- **Treat the harness as a variable with a price.** It is the one factor in your agent bill
  that you can change this afternoon, without touching model choice or prompt.
- **Measure cost per solved task, not cost per run.** A cheap harness that fails more often is
  not cheap. The study tracks this directly, and it is the column that settles arguments.
- **A thin harness is a legitimate starting point,** not a compromise you apologise for. Four
  tools is a serious baseline.
- **If you publish a model evaluation, name the harness.** A score without one is not a score
  for a model. It is a score for a pair, and the paired half is worth up to 5×.

## Where the result stops

This is a 30-task sample per benchmark with three attempts each, and the confidence intervals
are correspondingly wide — Claude Fable 5 on SWE-bench Lite lands somewhere in 91.1–100%.
Plenty of the success-rate differences above sit inside that noise. The cost differences do not;
they are large, consistent, and mechanically explained by the context measurements.

Both benchmarks are public, so the models may well have met them in training. Both also consist
of short, self-contained tasks — which is precisely the workload where heavy scaffolding has
least to offer. Subagents, long-horizon memory, permissions and hooks exist for multi-hour
sessions in a real repository, and a 30-task SWE-bench Lite sample does not measure any of that.
The authors say as much: richer harness features may still earn their keep on other models,
workloads and interaction settings, and harness complexity should be treated as an empirical
trade-off rather than assumed either way.

Finally, these are standardised API token prices. If you work behind a flat-rate subscription,
your marginal cost per attempt is somebody else's problem, and the tax is being paid on your
behalf rather than by you.

None of that dislodges the core observation. Whether a task gets solved is mostly about the
model. What it costs to solve is substantially about the harness — and that second number has
been going unreported, unbenchmarked, and unnoticed on the bill.
